lesson.title: Reading the Code: How DNA Sequencing Works
lesson.summary: DNA sequencing is the process of determining the exact order of nucleotides in a piece of DNA, the foundational technology behind modern genomics.
lesson.body:
DNA stores information in the order of its four bases, adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine, strung together along the double helix. Sequencing is simply the process of reading out that order, base by base, for a stretch of DNA that might be a single gene or an entire genome. It sounds straightforward, but doing it accurately, and doing it for the billions of bases in a genome, required real technological breakthroughs.

The first widely used method, developed by Frederick Sanger in the 1970s, is known as Sanger sequencing or the chain termination method. Without going deep into the chemistry, the general idea is that a DNA sample is copied using a mix of normal nucleotides and a small number of specially modified nucleotides that stop the growing DNA strand wherever they get incorporated. This produces a large collection of DNA fragments of every possible length, each one ending at a known base. Because gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size, running these fragments through a gel spreads them out from shortest to longest, and reading the fragments off in size order reveals the original sequence, letter by letter. Sanger sequencing was reliable enough that it was used to sequence the first human genome as part of the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, though it was slow and expensive by today's standards, and large scale sequencing depended on first amplifying DNA samples using PCR to have enough material to work with.

Starting in the 2000s, a family of newer techniques known as next generation sequencing, or NGS, transformed the field by sequencing millions of DNA fragments at the same time instead of one at a time. Without needing to detail the specific chemistry of any one platform, the key advance is massive parallelization, which cut the cost and time of sequencing a genome from years down to days, and eventually to hours. This shift is what made it practical to sequence not just one human genome as a landmark project, but thousands of genomes routinely, opening the door to the genome wide questions explored in genomics and the computational tools of bioinformatics covered next.
